t.3.1: Arjuna said: If you hold that understanding is superior to action, O Janārdana, then why do you urge me into this terrible deed, O Keśava?
t.3.3: The Blessed Lord said: In this world a twofold path was taught by me of old, O sinless one: for the Sāṃkhyas the yoga of knowledge, and for the yogins the yoga of action.
t.3.2: With words that seem mixed and contradictory, you seem to bewilder my understanding. Tell me decisively that one thing by which I may attain the highest good.
t.3.4: Not by abstaining from actions does a person attain freedom from action, nor by renunciation alone does he reach perfection.
t.3.5: For no one can ever remain even for a moment without performing action; everyone is helplessly made to act by the guṇas born of prakṛti.
t.3.6: He who restrains the organs of action but sits dwelling in his mind on the objects of the senses, deluded in himself, is called a hypocrite.
t.3.7: But he who, restraining the senses with the mind, O Arjuna, undertakes the yoga of action with the organs of action, unattached, he excels.
t.3.8: Perform your prescribed action, for action is superior to inaction. Even the maintenance of your body would not be accomplished if you were inactive.
t.3.9: Except for action done for the sake of sacrifice, this world is bound by action. For that purpose, O Kaunteya, perform action, freed from attachment.
t.3.11: With this nourish the gods, and may those gods nourish you; nourishing one another, you will attain the highest good.
t.3.10: In ancient times Prajāpati, having created beings together with sacrifice, said: “By this you shall bring forth increase; let this be for you the wish-fulfilling cow that yields what you desire.”
t.3.12: For the gods, nourished by sacrifice, will give you the enjoyments you desire. He who enjoys what they have given without offering anything to them in return is truly a thief.
t.3.13: The good, who eat what remains of the sacrifice, are released from all sins; but the wicked, who cook only for their own sake, eat sin itself.
t.3.14: From food all beings come into existence, and food arises from rain. Rain comes from sacrifice, and sacrifice is born of action.
t.3.15: Know that action arises from Brahman, and Brahman arises from the Imperishable; therefore the all-pervading Brahman is ever established in sacrifice.
t.3.16: He who here does not follow the wheel thus set in motion, whose life is sin and who delights in the senses, lives in vain, O Pārtha.
t.3.17: But the man who delights in the Self alone, who is satisfied in the Self, and who is content in the Self alone, for him there is no work that must be done.
t.3.18: For him there is no purpose whatsoever here in what is done, nor in what is left undone; nor does he depend on any being among all beings for any purpose.
t.3.19: Therefore, always unattached, perform the work that must be done; for by performing action without attachment, a man attains the Supreme.
t.3.20: Indeed, it was through action alone that Janaka and others attained perfection. Even with a view to the welfare of the world, you ought to act.
t.3.21: Whatever the best person does, that very thing other people do as well. Whatever standard he sets, the world follows that.
t.3.22: O Pārtha, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that I must do, nor anything unattained that I need to attain; and yet I remain engaged in action.
t.3.24: If I were not to perform action, these worlds would perish; I would be the author of confusion, and I would destroy these creatures.
t.3.25: As the unwise act attached to action, O Bhārata, so should the wise act unattached, desiring to bring about the welfare of the world.
t.3.26: The wise one should not unsettle the understanding of the ignorant who are attached to action; rather, remaining disciplined and performing all actions himself, he should lead them to delight in all works.
t.3.28: But the knower of the truth, O mighty-armed one, concerning the two divisions of the guṇas and their actions, thinking, "The guṇas move among the guṇas," does not become attached.
t.3.23: For if I were ever to cease engaging in action, unwearied, O Pārtha, men would follow my path in every way.
t.3.29: Those who are deluded by the guṇas of prakṛti become attached to the actions of the guṇas. One who knows the whole should not unsettle those dull ones whose knowledge is incomplete.
t.3.30: Renouncing all actions in me, with your mind fixed on the supreme Self, free from desire and free from possessiveness, fight with your fever of anguish gone.
t.3.31: Those men who constantly follow this teaching of mine, full of faith and without carping, they too are released from the bonds of actions.
t.3.27: Actions are in every way performed by the qualities of nature, yet one whose self is deluded by egoism thinks, 'I am the one who will do them.'
t.3.32: But those who, finding fault with this teaching of mine, do not follow it, know them to be deluded in all knowledge, senseless, and lost.
t.3.33: Even a man of knowledge acts in accordance with his own nature. All beings follow their nature; what will restraint accomplish?
t.3.34: Attraction and aversion are seated in the object of each and every sense. One should not come under the sway of these two, for they are his adversaries.
t.3.35: Better is one's own dharma, though lacking in merit, than the dharma of another well performed. Death in one's own dharma is better; the dharma of another brings fear.
t.3.36: Arjuna said: Then by what is a man impelled to commit sin, O Vārṣṇeya, even against his own will, as if compelled by force?
t.3.37: The Blessed Lord said: It is desire, it is anger, born of the guṇa of rajas; all-devouring and most sinful, know this to be the enemy here.
t.3.38: As fire is covered by smoke, as a mirror by dust, and as an embryo is enveloped by the womb, so is this covered by that.
t.3.40: The senses, the mind and the intellect are said to be its seat; through these it veils knowledge and deludes the embodied one.
t.3.39: The wise have their knowledge veiled by this constant enemy, O Kaunteya, which takes the form of desire and is an insatiable fire.
t.3.41: Therefore, O bull among the Bharatas, first restraining the senses, cast off this sinful one, the destroyer of knowledge and realization.
t.3.42: They say that the senses are superior; higher than the senses is the mind; higher than the mind is the intellect; but that which is beyond even the intellect is He.
t.3.43: Thus knowing that which is higher than the intellect, and steadying the self by the self, slay, O mighty-armed one, the enemy in the form of desire, so hard to overcome.
